claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a disordered BCC structure.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr exhibits high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has proven creep resistance up to approximately 1000 °C.
The proposed intervention is to replace Hf with enough Sc to produce approximately 10–15 at.% Sc in the alloy.
Replacing Hf with 10–15 at.% Sc will reduce alloy density by approximately 5–8%.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain or slightly improve tensile or yield strength at room temperature.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain or slightly improve tensile or yield strength at approximately 1000 °C.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain or slightly improve creep resistance at approximately 1000 °C.
The proposed property retention is conditional on preserving a disordered BCC matrix with controlled secondary-phase content.
Sc has a considerably lower density than Hf, so replacing Hf with Sc directly lowers the global alloy density.
The atomic-size mismatch introduced by Sc substitution enhances lattice distortion in the BCC matrix.
The additional lattice distortion increases dislocation pinning and thereby maintains alloy strength.
Inappropriate Sc substitution levels may form detrimental secondary phases that compromise high-temperature properties.
The proposed performance envelope extends from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under uniaxial loading.
Behavior after exposures longer than those tested or under non-uniaxial loading requires additional validation.
The hypothesis is rejected if density does not decrease by at least approximately 5% or if tensile strength or creep resistance at 1000 °C degrades significantly relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies 10–15 at.% Sc in the total alloy, whereas the experiment describes 10% and 15% replacement of the Hf inventory. For an equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr baseline, replacing 10–15% of Hf would yield only about 2–3 at.% Sc, not 10–15 at.% Sc, so the tested compositions are ambiguously or inconsistently defined.
